targetQuery: http protocol explained (methods, status codes, caching, cookies)
comparedAgainst: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods (MDN, fetched) — the article's likely comparator for safe/idempotent method classification. MDN presents the safe/idempotent/cacheable split almost entirely as a reference table with no narrative reasoning; the article instead builds a worked demonstration (PUT vs POST against an in-memory item store, showing stored state, not just status codes) and states the POST-safe-to-retry misconception MDN never addresses. No copied or paraphrased sentences found — the table's fact pattern (which methods are safe/idempotent) necessarily overlaps because it is the same RFC-defined fact, but wording and framing are original.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status (MDN, fetched) — comparator for the five status-code classes and 100 Continue. MDN's phrasing ('Client error responses', 'Server error responses') and the article's own table phrasing ('The server believes the request itself is at fault', 'The request was valid; the server failed anyway') are independently worded, not reworked from one another. The article adds something MDN does not: a live 100 Continue exchange with a real Expect header and a server that actually withholds the body read until it fires.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching and https://web.dev/articles/http-cache (fetched) — comparators for ETag/If-None-Match/304 and no-store. Both explain the same mechanism in different original language from the article ('the browser can skip the download' vs. the article's 'the resource is gone after either call' framing); no close paraphrase found. Disclosure: this session's WebSearch quota was exhausted after one query (200/200 used across the conversation before a planned search for a dedicated status-code reference site and a distinctive-sentence check on the PATCH/idempotent quote), so the third and fourth comparator legs rest on WebFetch reads of named URLs rather than a broader live search — flagged rather than presented as more thorough than it was.
justification:
Structurally and editorially this is strong, original work that is genuinely differentiated from its own pillar sibling: how-the-internet-works.md demonstrates the CLIENT side with TcpClient against a real host (example.com) and a one-off, single-purpose TcpListener capture rig used only to see what HttpClient puts on the wire (no method routing, no status families, no caching, no cookies). This article builds the SERVER side with TcpListener across five independently-themed programs (message framing, PUT/POST/GET against an in-memory store, four status-code families plus a real 1xx via Expect: 100-continue, SHA-256 ETag/If-None-Match/304, Set-Cookie/Cookie session with an attribute-stripping bug). I read both articles in full and confirm no helper, demo or running example is reused between them; the crosslinks file's 'Note for sibling writers' section (docs/crosslinks/networking/http-explained.md) accurately and specifically names what is now off-limits to tcp-vs-udp/tls-and-https/dns writers (the ReadHead/ReadBody mid-buffer blank-line scan, the PUT/POST item-store demo, the Expect: 100-continue round trip, the SHA-256 ETag/If-None-Match/304 demo, the cookie-attribute-stripping bug) — this is a genuinely useful coordination artifact, not filler. All 11 cited sources (RFC 9110, 9111, 9112, 9113, 9114, 9000, 7541, 9204, 6265, 5789, and Microsoft Learn's TcpListener.AcceptTcpClientAsync) are real and each is cited inline at least once; no source in front matter goes uncited and no in-body citation points to a source missing from front matter. Exercises are genuinely five different forms (a reasoning/prove-it on idempotency-by-luck-vs-by-design, an extend-the-code for HEAD, a prove-it on no-store precluding 304, a find-the-bug on verbatim cookie replay whose puzzle snippet is the bug itself rather than the diagnosis, and a closing count-what-changes exercise on HTTP/2 multiplexing) and none shows its output panel or answer before the collapsed solution. The toolchain sentence ('.NET 10 SDK (10.0.401) on Windows 11, x64') sits at the end of the opening paragraph, not as its first sentence, and is justified by the article's own claim that its output is fully deterministic (loopback, no timing measurements) rather than stamped as global provenance boilerplate. `node tools/run-code.mjs` independently confirms PASS, blocks=13, executed=6, matching the writer's claim exactly. No filler, no ad code, no keyword stuffing.

What holds this well below a pass is a real sourcing-accuracy problem the fabrication check was specifically asked to catch. In 'Telling a client its copy is still good', the article states: '`ETag` supplies a validator: an opaque token the server can recompute later and compare, defined once in RFC 9110 as identifying "one or more stored responses" ([section 8.8.3]).' I fetched RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 in full (the ETag definition and its 8.8.3.1 Generation subsection) and the quoted phrase 'one or more stored responses' does not appear anywhere in it; it does not appear anywhere in RFC 9110 at all. The phrase actually comes from RFC 9111 (Caching), used in an unrelated context (a cache invalidating stored responses after a successful DELETE/PUT, RFC 9111 sections 4.3.2/4.3.4). This is a quotation mark around text that was not said, attributed to a specific section that does not contain it — exactly the kind of fabricated-source-attribution the editorial brief's hard rule 1 and 3 forbid, not a paraphrase judgment call. Two adjacent citations in the same paragraph on idempotency have a related but lesser problem: 'Safe methods ... are idempotent by construction ([RFC 9110, section 9.2.1])' cites section 9.2.1, which defines 'safe' and never uses the word 'idempotent'; the actual sentence supporting that claim ('PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent') is in section 9.2.2, cited two sentences later for a different purpose. The follow-on claim that PUT and DELETE are 'idempotent anyway, each defined that way in its own section ([9.3.4], [9.3.5])' holds for PUT (9.3.4 states 'the intent of PUT is idempotent') but not for DELETE: I read all of section 9.3.5 and the word 'idempotent' never appears in it: DELETE's idempotency is established only by the general list in 9.2.2, not restated in its own section. None of this is a difference of interpretation; each is independently checkable against the RFC text I fetched and quoted above, and one of the three is a quotation mark placed around words the source never wrote. Given the article's entire premise is 'every status code, cache hit and cookie below comes from a real server, deterministic and checkable,' a reader who checks a footnote and finds the quoted text isn't there is exactly the failure mode AdSense review is meant to catch, and it caps this round well short of a pass regardless of the article's other strengths.

issues.location: "Telling a client its copy is still good" section: '`ETag` supplies a validator: an opaque token the server can recompute later and compare, defined once in RFC 9110 as identifying "one or more stored responses" ([section 8.8.3])'
issues.problem: The quoted phrase 'one or more stored responses' does not appear in RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 (verified by fetching the section's full text, including 8.8.3.1). It does not describe ETag anywhere in RFC 9110. The phrase is actually caching-invalidation language from RFC 9111 sections 4.3.2/4.3.4, in the unrelated context of a cache identifying which of its stored responses to update after a 304. This is a direct quotation attributed to a source that does not contain it.
issues.fixLooksLike: Drop the quotation marks and the false attribution. State the ETag definition in the article's own words (RFC 9110 8.8.3: 'an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource'), or quote that actual sentence instead.

issues.location: "Methods, and which ones are safe to repeat" section: 'Safe methods (the ones that should not change server state at all) are idempotent by construction ([RFC 9110, section 9.2.1])'
issues.problem: Section 9.2.1 (Safe Methods) defines 'safe' and never uses the word 'idempotent'. The sentence actually stating that safe methods are idempotent ('PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent') is in section 9.2.2, which the article cites two sentences later for the unrelated 9.2.2 client-retry point. The claim's own supporting text is in the section not cited for it.
issues.fixLooksLike: Move the section-9.2.1 citation to 9.2.2, or cite both (9.2.1 for the definition of 'safe', 9.2.2 for the idempotency claim about safe methods).

issues.location: Same paragraph: 'PUT and DELETE add nothing new but are idempotent anyway, each defined that way in its own section ([9.3.4], [9.3.5])'
issues.problem: True for PUT (RFC 9110 9.3.4 states 'the intent of PUT is idempotent'), but false for DELETE: I read all of section 9.3.5 and the word 'idempotent' never appears in it. DELETE's idempotency is established only by the general list in section 9.2.2, not restated in DELETE's own section, so the '[9.3.5]' citation does not support the clause it is attached to.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite 9.2.2 for DELETE's idempotency instead of 9.3.5, or rephrase to say only PUT restates it in its own section while DELETE's comes from the general list.
